corrected_value.title_o: Implicit Science Stereotypes Mediate the Relationship between Gender and Academic Participation

decisions.quote:
A Replication of Lane, Goh, and Driver-Linn ,2012: Predicting Plans to Pursue Science

Method

          Participants. Participants were volunteers at Project Implicit website (Nosek, 2005)

which were from the United States and born between 1994 and 1998. 514 participants

completed the experiment (68.48% women, Mage = 20.11, SDage = 1.28, 83.46% students).

Like Lane et al., we restricted the age of the participants to 18-22.
decisions.location: Appendix C, p. 1, lines 1759-1769 (and References, p. 26, lines 1258-1262)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind target 0 identify the same tested original study by Lane, Goh, and Driver-Linn (DOI 10.1007/s11199-011-0036-z, published online in 2011 and in print in 2012), which this paper directly replicates in Part 2 and Appendix C.

decisions.quote:
Replicating Lane et al., we

found significant advantage for the IAT (r = .245, p < .001) over explicit stereotypes (r =

.111, p = .012), Williams' t(511) = 2.304, p = .022, in predicting intentions to pursue the topic

stereotypically associated with the participant's gender. The bootstrap tests in the mediation-

like analyses found that controlling for attitudes significantly reduced the IAT's effect, b =

.168, SE = .028, 95% CI [0.114, 0.224], and the explicit stereotype's effect, b = .080, SE =

.030, 95% CI [0.019, 0.138]. The regression analyses showed that although the IAT's effect

was reduced, it remained significant, b = .067, SE = .032, t(511) = 2.132, p = .034, 95% CI

[0.005, 0.130], suggesting that attitudes might not be the only reason for the IAT/pursuit

relations. The explicit stereotype's effect was reduced to being non-significant, b = .010, SE =

.031, t(511) < 1, p = .755, 95% CI [-0.051, 0.070]. Importantly, we did not find evidence that

the IAT maintained its advantage over the explicit stereotypes after controlling for attitudes.

When we partialled out shared variance with attitudes, the IAT/pursuit relation (r = .095, p =

.032) was no longer reliably stronger than the explicit stereotype/pursuit relation (r = .019, p

= .662), Williams' t(511) = 1.251, p = .212.
decisions.location: Part 2: Predicting Plans to Pursue Science, p. 15, lines 728-756
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree on 'statistically successful but flawed'. In the full replication sample (N = 514), the authors statistically replicate Lane et al.'s original finding that the gender-science IAT predicts academic pursuit intentions significantly better than explicit stereotypes (Williams' t(511) = 2.304, p = .022; an exploratory freshman-only subset failure is explicitly dismissed in Appendix C as random error from small sample size). However, the paper's central thesis is that comparing the gender-science IAT to explicit stereotype measures is confounded because the IAT captures personal attraction/liking toward science, and once shared variance with attitudes is partialled out, the IAT's predictive advantage over explicit stereotypes disappears (Williams' t(511) = 1.251, p = .212).

decisions.quote:
Following that logic, we re-analyzed data from

one previous study (Nosek & Smyth, 2011) and replicated another (Lane et al., 2012) to

examine what happens to the advantage of the gender-science IAT over self-report measures

in predicting a science-relevant outcome, when attitudes are added to the model.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding agree that the study of Lane et al. (2012) is a replication: the authors collected new data from a fresh sample of 514 Project Implicit participants using Lane et al.'s materials and procedure to re-test their finding.

corrected_value.authors: Nosek, B. A., & Smyth, F. L.
corrected_value.title: Implicit social cognitions predict sex differences in math engagement and achievement.

decisions.quote:
Nosek and Smyth (2011) compared the gender-science IAT and the explicit

stereotype (measured with two self-reported items: Men are better at math than women are

and Women can achieve as much as men in math) in predicting math-related outcomes. We

re-analyzed that data and found only one variable, the difference between math and verbal

SAT scores, that had reliably stronger relation with the IAT (r = .193, p < .001) than the

explicit stereotype (r = .090, p = .004), Williams' t(1040) = 2.590, p = .010.
decisions.reason: In Part 2 of the full text (pp. 13–14, lines 387–441; Discussion p. 18, lines 536–547), the authors explicitly re-analyze the original dataset of Nosek and Smyth (2011; full citation in References p. 27, lines 803–806: Nosek, B. A., & Smyth, F. L. (2011). Implicit social cognitions predict sex differences in math engagement and achievement. American Educational Research Journal, 48(5), 1125-1156. doi: 10.3102/0002831211410683) to test whether the gender-science IAT's advantage over explicit stereotypes in predicting math-related outcomes (specifically the math-minus-verbal SAT difference score, r = .193 vs. r = .090, Williams' t(1040) = 2.590, p = .010) persists when controlling for self-reported math attitudes (finding the partial correlations r = .049 vs. r = .017 no longer significantly differ, Williams' t(1040) < 1, p = .442). Because this re-analyzes Nosek and Smyth's (2011) original data to test the robustness of their reported finding, it is an actual empirical reproduction (`record_type: "reproduction"`). The only shipped row for this paper is row 1499 (Lane, Goh, & Driver-Linn, 2011/2012, 'Implicit Science Stereotypes Mediate the Relationship between Gender and Academic Participation', DOI `10.1007/s11199-011-0036-z`), which corresponds to sibling target 0 (replicated with a new sample of N = 514 in Part 2, pp. 14–15 and Appendix C) and is a completely distinct work from Nosek and Smyth (2011). Per review instructions when no paper outcome is requested, `outcome` is set to `cannot_be_determined`.
